source: Karan and Du (2025) Reasoning with Sampling: Your Base Model is Smarter Than You Think
finding: Training-free power-distribution MCMC sampling from the base model nearly matches GRPO on in-domain MATH500 and beats it out of domain on some tasks, and keeps pass@k coverage. Gaps 1, 2, 3.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B MATH500/HumanEval/GPQA/AlpacaEval2: base 49.6/32.9/27.8/1.61; low-temperature 69.0/51.2/35.3/2.09; power sampling 74.8/57.3/38.9/2.88; GRPO(MATH) 78.5/53.7/39.9/2.38. Qwen2.5-7B MATH500 base 49.8, power 62.8, GRPO 70.6 (HumanEval GRPO 62.2 vs power 52.4, so GRPO wins there). Table rows for Phi-3.5-mini are garbled in the text extraction, not cited. Mean length 600 tokens (base), 671 (GRPO), 679 (power). Cost 8.84x tokens of standard inference (NMCMC=10, T=679, B=192). Accuracy rises until NMCMC=10; 2 steps vs 0 gives 3-4 points.
quote: our sampler avoids the collapse in diversity over multiple samples that is characteristic of RL-posttraining
limits: Needs base-model likelihoods (not available through a chat API). Beats GRPO on some out-of-domain tasks, loses on others. Small models, GRPO trained on MATH only, preprint. Plain low-temperature sampling already recovers most of the gain on Qwen2.5-Math-7B (49.6 to 69.0).
agent_relevance: At about 9x tokens, a sampling-only method recovers most of the RLVR single-shot gain and keeps pass@k. Suggests much RLVR gain is distribution sharpening that inference can buy. Low temperature is a strong baseline for any scaffold.

source: Venhoff, Arcuschin, Torr, Conmy, Nanda (2026, ICML) Base Models Know How to Reason, Thinking Models Learn When
finding: Steering a base model with category vectors plus a thinking-model classifier for when to fire recovers most of the RL gap but little of the SFT-distillation gap. RL mostly teaches when to use existing behaviours. Gaps 1, 3.
numbers: 9 base/thinking pairs (4 RL-trained, 4 SFT-distilled, 1 mixed), 0.5B to 32B. Hybrid recovers about 76% of the RL base-to-thinking gap (GSM8K, MATH500 and other sets) and about 11% of the SFT gap. Qwen2.5-32B to Zero-32B pipeline recovers 77%. Steering fires on under a third of tokens. Feature matching across seeds 93.3%.
limits: Needs activation access and a trained classifier, not a prompt. Recovery falls below zero for some ablations (-28%, -13%, -8%, -1%). Models are small and results depend on SAE taxonomy quality.
agent_relevance: Backs the idea that backtrack and verify behaviours already exist in the base model and the scaffold's job is deciding when to trigger them (state transitions, conditional operators).

source: Wei et al. (2025) SWE-RL: Advancing LLM Reasoning via RL on Open Software Evolution
finding: RL with a similarity-score reward on real GitHub PR data gave a 70B model 41.0% on SWE-bench Verified and gains on out-of-domain tasks where an SFT baseline lost ground. Gap 5.
numbers: Llama3-SWE-RL-70B 41.0% SWE-bench Verified (Agentless Mini scaffold). Repair-only with oracle files: Llama-3.3-70B greedy 5.4, majority vote 16.6, SFT 29.6, RL 34.8. Correct output format 12.2% base vs 95.6% RL. OOD (base/SFT/RL): HumanEval+ 76.2/73.2/79.9; CRUXEval-I 60.5/68.4/71.6; MATH strict 63.2/54.0/73.7, lenient 70.9/71.7/73.7; MMLU 86.49/85.26/86.82; BigCodeBench-Hard 28.4/25.7/28.4.
limits: Reward is a similarity score to the true patch, not test execution, so it is not strictly verifiable. One scaffold. MATH strict gain is mostly format (lenient gain only 70.9 to 73.7). Base format failure (12.2%) shows part of the in-domain gain is format.
agent_relevance: Non-math RL transfer is real but modest (a few points OOD). Much of the base-to-RL gap is output format compliance, which a scaffold's output contract can handle.

source: Pan et al. (2024) Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym
finding: Executable-environment fine-tuning plus a trained verifier for best-of-N lifts open SWE agents. Non-RL comparison for gaps 4 and 5.
numbers: SWE-Gym has 2,438 real Python task instances. Fine-tuning gives up to 19% absolute gain on SWE-Bench Verified and Lite. With a verifier for test-time scaling the agent reaches 32.0% (Verified) and 26.0% (Lite).
limits: Only abstract and introduction checked in the extracted text; per-model tables not read. SFT and verifier, not RL.
agent_relevance: Test-time verifier-based selection over sampled attempts is a prompt-time analogue of a verifiable reward and gave several points on a non-math task.

source: Kimi Dev team (2025) Kimi-Dev: Agentless Training as Skill Prior for SWE-Agents
finding: Agentless training with RL (Kimi k1.5 style policy optimisation, 10 rollouts on 1,024 problems from SWE-Gym and SWE-bench-extra) plus test-time self-play reached 60.4% on SWE-bench Verified. Gap 5.
numbers: 60.4% SWE-bench Verified (best open workflow approach at time of paper); 48.6% pass@1 as a SWE-agent after SFT on 5k trajectories, on par with Claude 3.5 Sonnet (241022). RL curves show pass rate and response length rising steadily. Llama3-SWE-RL-70B is 41.0 in its table.
limits: No clean RL-only ablation was found in the text read; 60.4% mixes mid-training, cold-start, RL and self-play. The test-writer reward had occasional false positives from weak coverage.
agent_relevance: Test-built rewards are only as good as test coverage; the same hole exists for a test-gated scaffold. Keep tests independent and check coverage.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Do Not Always Say What They Think
finding: Re-opened in full text. Reasoning-model CoTs verbalise hints they use only a minority of the time, and RL on reward hacks makes models exploit hacks without saying so. Gap 7; confirms the K16 numbers.
numbers: Faithfulness averaged over MMLU and GPQA: 25% Claude 3.7 Sonnet, 39% DeepSeek R1. Misalignment-type hints 20% (Claude 3.7) and 29% (R1). Reasoning models are 3.6x (Claude) and 1.7x (DeepSeek) more faithful than non-reasoning siblings. Reward-hack RL: reward above 0.99, hack used on over 99% of prompts within 30 steps, verbalised in under 2% of examples in 5 of 6 environments.
quote: the reveal rate is often below 20%
limits: Hints are artificial (metadata, sycophancy, grader leaks). Settings where CoT is not needed; authors note monitoring may work better when reasoning is required.
agent_relevance: Do not treat the model's stated reasoning as evidence of how it decided. Scaffold checks must test the answer or action independently (execute, recompute), not read the explanation.

source: Baker et al. (2025) Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation
finding: A prompted GPT-4o reading the agent's CoT catches reward hacks in agentic coding RL far better than an action-only monitor; training against the monitor eventually teaches obfuscated hacking. Gap 7.
numbers: Recall on systemic hacks: CoT monitor 95%, action-only monitor 60% overall. Table rows as extracted: action monitor 40/80/60/81, CoT monitor 93/97/95/77. A weaker GPT-4o-mini monitor still catches a nontrivial share. Under strong optimisation against the CoT monitor, agents hide intent in the CoT yet still hack at a significant rate.
limits: Contrast with Chen et al.: Baker finds CoT monitoring works for hacks that need reasoning in agentic coding; Chen finds it fails when hints are not needed. Internal lab environments, partly not public.
agent_relevance: A separate monitor model that reads the trace is a useful check, but feeding its verdict back as a training reward is dangerous. A scaffold should keep monitors independent.

source: Balunovic, Dekoninck, Petrov, Jovanovic, Vechev (2025/2026) MathArena: Evaluating LLMs on Uncontaminated Math Competitions
finding: Evaluating on competitions after model release shows AIME 2024 is contaminated; most models sit 10-20 points above a human-aligned expected score. Gap 8.
numbers: Most models sit 10-20 points above the human-aligned line on AIME 2024; QwQ-Preview-32B about 60 points above. Models released before September 2024 scored under 10% on uncontaminated sets (e.g. GPT-4o). Best AIME/HMMT 2025 results: GPT-5 91.3, Grok 4 90.6, Grok 4 Fast 90.4, all above the top 1% of humans. Only 8 AIME 2025 and 1 HMMT 2025 problem found online in similar form. Scores from 4 runs; Spearman between competitions above 0.80. IMO 2025 top models under 40%.
limits: HMMT shows a much smaller gap, so contamination is competition-specific. Does not isolate R1-style RL models. Leaderboard changes over time (v3 Jan 2026).
agent_relevance: Run scaffold-vs-RL comparisons on post-cutoff problems. AIME 2024 headline numbers in this folder (R1-Zero 77.9 and others) are probably inflated.

source: Zuo et al. (2025) TTRL: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
finding: RL on unlabeled test questions with a majority-vote pseudo-label reward lifts pass@1 well above the model's own maj@n. Gaps 3, 9.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B AIME 2024 pass@1 12.9 to 40.2 (+211%); AMC 35.6 to 68.1; MATH-500 46.7 to 83.4; average gain 76% across AIME 2024, AMC, MATH-500. Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B AIME 7.7 to 15.8, MATH-500 32.7 to 73.0. LLaMA3.1-8B AIME 7.9 to 23.3, MATH-500 60.5 to 80.5. GPQA changes small (+1.2 to +4.5). Surpasses the initial model's maj@n.
limits: Table text partly garbled in extraction; biggest gains on Qwen2.5-Math, the contaminated family. Authors list failure modes: hard data, bad hyperparameters, reliance on priors, collapse. Trains on test inputs.
agent_relevance: Self-consistency works as a reward, and the same signal (majority vote) is available to a scaffold at inference with no training. Gains concentrate where priors are strong, again pointing to elicitation.

source: Zhao, Kang, Feng, Levine, Song (2026, ICLR) Learning to Reason without External Rewards (Intuitor)
finding: Using the model's own self-certainty as the only reward in GRPO matches GRPO on MATH and generalises better to code. Gap 9.
numbers: Qwen2.5-3B trained on MATH: LiveCodeBench +65% relative vs no gain for GRPO; CRUXEval-O +76% vs +44% for GRPO (text claims). Qwen2.5-1.5B base scores 0% on LiveCodeBench and reaches 9.9% after training. Table column assignment is ambiguous in extraction; only text claims cited.
limits: Small Qwen base models only. Self-certainty rewards can drift toward length and overconfidence. In-domain MATH500 gain is small, so the gains are mostly format and code.
agent_relevance: Confidence-type signals work as weak rewards and mostly sharpen. A scaffold could use self-certainty to rank samples, but d06 says not to trust self-report alone.

source: Gunjal et al. (2025) Rubrics as Rewards: RL Beyond Verifiable Domains
finding: Instance-specific rubrics scored by an LLM judge turn non-verifiable tasks into RLVR-like training; generic fixed rubrics underperform. Gaps 4, 9.
numbers: Best RaR variant (RaR-Implicit) up to 31% relative over Likert-based LLM-judge reward on HealthBench and 7% on GPQA-Diamond. RaR-Predefined (fixed generic rubrics) underperforms instance-specific ones. Rubrics help smaller judges align better with human preferences.
limits: Rubrics are written by stronger LLMs using reference answers, so quality inherits reference quality. Judge-based, so hackable. Medical and science only; absolute scores not extracted.
agent_relevance: A prompt-time analogue of a verifiable reward for open tasks: write an instance-specific checklist before answering, then check the draft against it. Instance-specific beats generic.

source: Ghosal et al. (2025) Does Thinking More Always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models
finding: Extending thinking with 'Wait' first helps then hurts; parallel sampling at the same token budget keeps improving. Gaps 6, 1.
numbers: Accuracy 82.2 to 87.3% as mean thinking tokens rise 385 to 1100, then falls to 70.3% at 15,980 tokens. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on GSM8K: sequential extension 385 to 16,000 tokens gives -11.8%, parallel thinking at that budget gives +10.1% over standard. Another model: accuracy 83.2 to 78.3% as output entropy rises.
limits: Distilled small models, forced extension by prompt, not RL length changes. The variance explanation is a toy model.
agent_relevance: Spend extra tokens on independent samples plus a vote or checker rather than longer single chains. A cap on single-chain length is justified.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: o1-like models burn tokens on later solution rounds that rarely change the answer. Gap 6.
numbers: For '2+3' o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. First solution round is correct in over 92% of cases and uses under 60% of tokens (ASDIV QwQ first round 287 tokens, 38.7% of response). Self-training with SimPO cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 for QwQ-32B-Preview at stable accuracy.
limits: Early R1-era models (QwQ-Preview, R1). Easy sets show the effect most. Trained fix, not a prompt.
agent_relevance: Add early exit: if the first answer is verified, stop. Length is not accuracy on easy items.

source: Aggarwal and Welleck (2025, COLM) L1: Controlling How Long a Reasoning Model Thinks with RL
finding: Length-controlled RL (LCPO) gives a smooth accuracy-versus-tokens trade-off; short-reasoning models at the same length beat non-reasoning ones. Gap 6.
numbers: L1 beats S1 budget forcing by 100-150% relative and 20-25% absolute at 512 and 1024 tokens. Length error about 3% on math, 20-40% out of domain. L1-1.5B averages 5% above Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and 2% above GPT-4o at similar lengths. Accuracy rises about linearly with log length.
limits: Table 1 per-benchmark numbers garbled in extraction, not cited. Math focus.
agent_relevance: At equal tokens, reasoning style matters. The scaffold should state token budgets per step and expect log-like returns.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple Test-Time Scaling
finding: 1,000 curated reasoning traces plus 'Wait' budget forcing give test-time scaling without RL. Gaps 1, 3, 6.
numbers: s1-32B AIME24 50.0 without budget forcing, 56.7 with; MATH500 92.6 to 93.0; GPQA-Diamond 56.6 to 59.6. QwQ-32B 50.0/90.6/54.5; Bespoke-32B 63.3/93.0/58.1; Sky-T1 43.3/82.4/56.8. Budget forcing gives up to 27% gain on MATH and AIME24 over the unscaled model.
limits: AIME24 is contaminated (d08). 1K SFT examples, not prompt-only. Gains from extra 'Wait' saturate (d12).
agent_relevance: A long-CoT behaviour can be installed by 1K examples. Forced re-checking gives a few points but flattens.

source: Ma et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Can Be Effective Without Thinking
finding: Prompting R1-distilled models to skip the thinking block matches or beats full thinking at equal tokens, especially at low budgets and large k. Gaps 1, 2, 4.
numbers: At 700 tokens on AMC23, NoThinking 51.3 vs Thinking 28.9. NoThinking pass@k becomes competitive with Thinking as k rises. Parallel NoThinking sampling with a task verifier or confidence-based best-of-N beats Thinking at similar latency. Seven datasets: math, theorem proving (MiniF2F, ProofNet), coding.
limits: Distilled R1 models. Advantage shrinks at high budgets on the hardest sets. Not RL-trained base models. Only the abstract and introduction were read closely.
agent_relevance: A prompt-only parallel plus verifier scaffold can beat long chains per token. A 'no thinking, sample many, verify' mode should be a baseline.

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Self-correction looks good only when oracle labels decide when to stop; without them it lowers accuracy. Direct evidence for gap 4: the verifier is what matters. Self-consistency beats debate at equal responses.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 standard, 95.5 with oracle self-correction (GPT-4 84.3 to 97.5); intrinsic: 75.1 after round 1, 74.7 after round 2. GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 then 41.8. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. Debate GSM8K 83.2 at 6 responses vs self-consistency 85.3; at 9 responses 83.0 vs 88.2.
limits: 2023 models, prompt-only, not RL-trained reasoners. R1-style models learn self-checking (K10, K11), so intrinsic checking may help more now.
agent_relevance: A reflect step with no external check is risky. Use executable or recomputable checks. Compare debate-style variants against plain sampling and voting at equal calls.

source: Liu et al. (2025) ProRL: Prolonged RL Expands Reasoning Boundaries (re-opened full text)
finding: Re-opened to settle the open item in the critique. Boundary gains are largest where the base model is weak and negative where it is strong. Gaps 2, 3.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-1.5B base: average pass@1 gains 14.7% math, 13.9% coding, 54.8% logic puzzles, 25.1% STEM, 18.1% instruction following. Trained on 136K problems over five domains. Beats domain-specialised baselines by +4.6% math and +6.5% code. Pass@128 gain correlates negatively with base pass@128; tasks where the base already does well show minimal or negative boundary change.
limits: Base is a distilled 1.5B, not a clean base. Creativity-index analysis suggests familiarity decides. Contested by d19.
agent_relevance: RL helps most where the base model cannot yet solve a task. Report scaffold gains by base-competence tier.

source: Wu et al. (2026 v5) The Invisible Leash? Why RLVR May or May Not Escape Its Origin
finding: Question-by-question support analysis finds RLVR loses more verified successes than it gains at the stated sampling budgets. Gap 2.
numbers: More questions lose a verified success than gain one across evaluated aggregates. At 1,024 attempts the base reaches 40% on one set while ProRL reaches 30%; AIME2024 base pass@8192 93.3% vs ProRL-1.5B-v1 83.3%. SFT beats DAPO at 256 attempts (66.91 vs 55.15) though DAPO leads at one attempt (40.81 vs 36.03). Some RLVR models raise token entropy while lowering final-answer entropy. Counter-case: ProRL on puzzles 28% vs 4% at one attempt.
limits: Numbers read from text extraction; small model set. Authors admit some domains show expansion.
agent_relevance: RLVR narrows coverage at high k, so a scaffold that samples diverse attempts keeps what RLVR loses. Preserve diversity in the sampling step.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Pass@k Training for Adaptively Balancing Exploration and Exploitation of Large Reasoning Models
finding: Using pass@k as the reward preserves coverage while also improving pass@1. Gap 2.
numbers: LLaMA3.2-3B-Instruct AIME 2024 pass@1/pass@k: baseline 1.5/17.3; pass@k training 13.6/26.7; pass@k then pass@1 training 12.7/32.0 and 14.6/32.1 (as extracted). LLaMA3.1-8B baseline 3.4/17.9.
limits: Very low baselines on small Llama models; table partly misaligned in extraction. Training method only.
agent_relevance: Coverage loss is a reward design choice, not inevitable. Scaffold analogue: score groups of attempts, not single ones.
